The first time I saw the ocean, I was eight years old, standing on a weathered wooden pier in Maine. The water stretched endlessly, shifting from deep blue to turquoise under the afternoon sun, and I remember thinking it was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen—not just because of its color, but because it felt alive. The waves whispered against the pilings, the gulls screamed overhead, and for a moment, I forgot about everything else: school, chores, the way my little brother had just tripped me. The ocean didn’t care about any of that. It just *was*.

Years later, I still find myself drawn to things that feel infinite—the way a forest hums with unseen life, the way a book can pull you into another world, the quiet magic of a city street at midnight when the lights blur together. There’s something comforting in the unknown, in the things we can’t control. Maybe that’s why I love stories—whether they’re true or made up—because they remind us that meaning isn’t always neat or logical. Sometimes it’s messy, like the tide pulling in and out, leaving behind shells and seaweed and the occasional lost sandcastle.

I don’t know if I’ll ever write something profound, but I like the idea of leaving a trail of words behind me, like breadcrumbs for someone else to follow. Maybe they’ll find what they’re looking for. Maybe they won’t. But the searching itself feels important.

Right now, I’m sitting in a café with a half-empty mug of coffee gone cold, watching raindrops slide down the window. It’s ordinary, but it’s also *this*—a snapshot of a moment that won’t last, and that’s okay. The ocean is still out there, waiting. And so am I.
